cim: Artificial intelligence and the erosion of human agency
cim_eredeti: Artificial intelligence and the erosion of human agency
szoveg_eredeti:
Oct. 27 (UPI) -- Latin America is racing to measure its readiness for artificial intelligence. But there is another question that cannot be answered by counting data centers or national strategies. Are its citizens retaining the ability to question the systems on which they increasingly depend?

On Oct. 20, Chile's National Center for Artificial Intelligence (CENIA) and the U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) released the fourth Latin American Artificial Intelligence Index (ILIA), assessing 20 countries.

Chile again ranks first, followed by Brazil and Uruguay. Eleven of the 20 countries now include AI-related content in school curricula, up from two in 2024, and 85% have or are developing national AI strategies, though only Brazil and Colombia explicitly budget for implementing them.

Yet technological readiness is not the same as human agency, meaning the capacity to act intentionally, reflect on choices and accept responsibility for them.

AI can extend that capacity. It can also erode it when people surrender decision-making without understanding how they are made. As we contemplate the possibility of artificial general intelligence or systems surpassing humans in economically valuable tasks, the essential question is not only what machines can do, but what we may cease to do for ourselves.

The distinction is rooted in the work of Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela. They described living systems as autopoietic, meaning self-producing and self-maintaining. Human agency arises within embodied life, formed by consciousness, vulnerability and relationships.

AI systems, by contrast, are allopoietic. They are designed and sustained through processes outside themselves, producing results rather than reproducing themselves as living organisms.

This does not mean AI is powerless or incapable of increasingly autonomous action in a functional sense. It means that computational performance is distinct from human agency, which carries ethical judgment and moral responsibility. An algorithm may recommend a decision; it cannot relieve the person or institution using it of accountability.

Psychologist Albert Bandura linked agency to intention, forethought and self-reflection. Sociologists Margaret Archer and Pierpaolo Donati emphasized another dimension: people develop judgment through inner deliberation and relationships with others.

We are not merely consumers of information. We are persons, who influence, and are influenced by, our families, communities and institutions.

Yet the design of many digital platforms pushes us in the opposite direction. Infinite scrolling and variable rewards capture attention. Recommendation systems narrow the alternatives we see. Automatic answers tempt us to skip the effort of interpretation. Opaque systems make it difficult to discover why we were rejected or steered toward a particular choice.

I call the result "agency starvation," a gradual weakening of attention and deliberation. No one necessarily takes away our judgment. We simply stop exercising it.

A 2025 study by Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University, based on reports from 319 knowledge workers, found that greater confidence in generative AI was associated with less reported critical-thinking effort, while greater confidence in one's own abilities was associated with more.

The study does not prove that AI causes diminished judgment, but it illuminates the danger of trusting an answer because checking it is inconvenient.

The consequences go beyond personal habits. When an algorithm influences access to work, credit or social benefits, a citizen must be able to ask why and receive a meaningful answer.

Chilean legal scholar Viviana Ponce de León has warned that a gap in the country's revised data protection legislation could allow public agencies to escape human-review safeguards for automated decisions. The reform is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 1, though the government has asked Congress to postpone it until December 2027.

California courts have confronted related questions of responsibility arising from increasingly powerful digital technologies. In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent for designing platforms to hook young users. Both companies said they would appeal, but the verdict could influence thousands of similar lawsuits.

Meanwhile, appellate courts have sanctioned lawyers who filed AI-generated briefs with fabricated citations. In a 2025 California appellate decision, Noland v. Land of the Free, the court fined an attorney $10,000 for submitting AI-generated fabricated citations and warned that lawyers must personally verify the authorities they cite.

In both cases, responsibility fell on the people who built or used the technology, not on the technology itself.

What would an alternative look like? I propose an Eco-Ethical-Systemic-Relational approach to AI, grounded in four connected dimensions.

The ecological or vital dimension recognizes the limits of human attention and the need for technology that respects our biological rhythms rather than exploiting them. The systemic dimension treats technology as part of society, calling for transparent, auditable systems and safeguards against concentrations of algorithmic power.

The relational dimension puts empathy and shared responsibility ahead of connectivity for its own sake. Families, schools, professional associations and local communities are where the habits of questioning and deliberation are formed, habits that no government policy can create by decree.

The ethical dimension rests on two principles. Cognitive sovereignty means retaining control over the processes by which we understand and judge the world. Technological subsidiarity means using AI to assist human action without displacing human ethical or professional responsibility.

If an automated system recommends denying someone a benefit, an accountable human decision-maker should remain available to review, explain and, when necessary, correct that decision.

These principles do not demand resistance to innovation. They demand that progress be measured not only by speed or investment, but also by whether people become more capable of exercising freedom and responsibility.

The question is no longer whether Latin America will adopt AI. It already has. The question is whether its citizens will retain the knowledge, confidence and right to challenge decisions made in their name.

The greatest danger is not simply that machines may one day think like humans. It is that humans may grow accustomed to acting like machines, accepting instructions without reflection. In an age of increasingly powerful algorithms, the freedom to ask why may become one of democracy's most important safeguards.

Carlos Cantero Ojeda, a Chilean academic at the International University of La Rioja in Spain, is the author of "Sociedad digital: razón y emoción" ("Digital Society: Reason and Emotion"). He lectures and consults internationally on ethics, social innovation, human development and how people adapt to digital society. The views and opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author.
